verses.text: Then Zophar the Naamathite answered,
“Therefore do my thoughts give answer to me, even by reason of my haste that is in me.
I have heard the reproof which puts me to shame. The spirit of my understanding answers me.
Don’t you know this from old time, since man was placed on earth,
that the triumphing of the wicked is short, the joy of the godless but for a moment?
Though his height mount up to the heavens, and his head reach to the clouds,
yet he shall perish forever like his own dung. Those who have seen him shall say, ‘Where is he?’
He shall fly away as a dream, and shall not be found. Yes, he shall be chased away like a vision of the night.
The eye which saw him shall see him no more, neither shall his place any more see him.
His children shall seek the favor of the poor. His hands shall give back his wealth.
His bones are full of his youth, but youth shall lie down with him in the dust.
“Though wickedness is sweet in his mouth, though he hide it under his tongue,
though he spare it, and will not let it go, but keep it still within his mouth;
yet his food in his bowels is turned. It is cobra venom within him.
He has swallowed down riches, and he shall vomit them up again. God will cast them out of his belly.
He shall suck cobra venom. The viper’s tongue shall kill him.
He shall not look at the rivers, the flowing streams of honey and butter.
That for which he labored he shall restore, and shall not swallow it down. According to the substance that he has gotten, he shall not rejoice.
For he has oppressed and forsaken the poor. He has violently taken away a house, and he shall not build it up.
“Because he knew no quietness within him, he shall not save anything of that in which he delights.
There was nothing left that he didn’t devour, therefore his prosperity shall not endure.
In the fullness of his sufficiency, distress shall overtake him. The hand of everyone who is in misery shall come on him.
When he is about to fill his belly, God will cast the fierceness of his wrath on him. It will rain on him while he is eating.
He shall flee from the iron weapon. The bronze arrow shall strike him through.
He draws it out, and it comes out of his body. Yes, the glittering point comes out of his liver. Terrors are on him.
All darkness is laid up for his treasures. An unfanned fire shall devour him. It shall consume that which is left in his tent.
The heavens shall reveal his iniquity. The earth shall rise up against him.
The increase of his house shall depart. They shall rush away in the day of his wrath.
This is the portion of a wicked man from God, the heritage appointed to him by God.”

footnotes.content: Zophar breaks in—he cannot hold his peace any longer. Sometimes a hurried tongue speaks truth, sometimes bitter presumption; the good Lord knows which.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He feels the urgency in his own spirit, as if the words will burst out if he doesn't speak them. Haste can be the voice of anger, or the voice of conviction; Zophar is certain he has wisdom to share.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Job's words have stung him to shame, yet rather than question his own theology, Zophar calls on his intellect to answer back. A proud heart defends itself before it bows.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zophar appeals to ancient knowledge—what has been known since men dwelt upon earth. He sees the doctrine of retribution as immemorial truth, woven into creation itself. Yet the Lord sometimes answers differently than we expect.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The core of Zophar's claim: wicked joy is brief, a moment only. There is truth here, though incomplete—the Lord's mercy is endless, and His patience with the sinner is mysterious.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even if wickedness reaches heaven-high, even if the wicked lift their head with pride—the image speaks to the human heart's desperate climb. The Lord sees from above, and His view is always final.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zophar's language turns brutal: perish like dung, forgotten utterly. Yet I'm reminded that the deepest shame is not to be forgotten, but to stand before the Lord unforgiven. That is the final word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The wicked shall vanish as a dream, swift and insubstantial. Sometimes I wonder if Zophar speaks truly—yet I know the vanity he names is real. Only in Jesus do we find substance that lasts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The eye that sees him shall see no more—erasure, utter removal. Yet the Lord's eye never forgets His own. That is the comfort: we are seen, known, held by One who will never turn away.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The wicked man's children must beg, his own hands forced to give back what he stole. There is a justice here—though I've learned that the Lord's justice is more tender than mere reversal; He restores what sin has broken.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His bones, full of youthful vigor, shall lie down in dust beside him. Youth and strength cannot save us; only the Lord's hand can. In age or youth, we are safe only in His grip.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Wickedness is sweet in the mouth—Zophar names the seduction plainly. Sin tastes good to the willful heart. Yet the Lord teaches us that His way, though it costs us comfort, feeds the soul.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He hides it, clings to it, will not release it—the image of a man holding poison in his mouth. Repentance begins when we finally, finally let go and cry out to the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: What was sweet turns to venom within him—the wages of sin working in flesh and spirit. The Lord permits sin's bitter fruit, that we might learn His way is the way of life.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He swallows riches and must vomit them up—he cannot keep what he devoured. The Lord will cast it out of him. How often I see this in the soul: we cannot hold what we grasp without Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Cobra venom, the viper's tongue—death delivered by the very thing he fed himself on. The symmetry is terrible: the wicked perish by their own appetite.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rivers of honey and butter—images of abundance he shall never enjoy. He has made himself unable to taste joy. The Lord alone can heal that deadened palate.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All his labor must be restored; he cannot swallow it down or rejoice in it. There is judgment here, yet I see also the Lord's call to restitution—a path back to Him for any who will repent.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He oppressed the poor, seized houses violently. Zophar names a specific sin: the abuse of the weak. The Lord hears the cry of the poor, and He will answer.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: No quietness within him—the wicked man's interior is turbulent, his restlessness his own jailer. Yet the Lord offers peace that passes understanding, even to the guilty soul who turns.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He devoured everything, yet it sustained nothing; his prosperity cannot endure. How true—all that is built on wickedness crumbles. Only what the Lord builds stands eternal.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When fullness comes, distress strikes; hands of the miserable reach out to him. The pattern holds: the wicked cannot fill themselves; judgment comes when they think themselves safe.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God's fierceness shall rain upon him while he eats—His wrath comes not in abstraction but in the moment of false security. The Lord's justice is swift and total.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Iron weapon, bronze arrow—the imagery moves from internal corruption to external judgment. Zophar sees in the wicked man no escape, no shelter from God's hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The arrow pierces through him, exits from his liver—violence and terror are his end. Yet I remember that Jesus bore the arrow, the wrath, the piercing. In Him, the judgment turns toward mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All darkness is laid up for his treasures; unfanned fire devours what remains. The wicked man's end is thorough—no redemption, no refuge. Yet the Lord's way is always to call the wandering home.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Heaven and earth shall reveal his iniquity, rise up against him. The creation itself becomes witness to his guilt. Yet we know that in Jesus, creation is being restored—renewed, not merely condemned.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His household wealth shall depart in the day of His wrath—sudden, complete, inescapable. Yet the Lord's wrath is never arbitrary; it is the final word upon those who refuse His call to repent.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zophar closes with certainty: this is the wicked man's portion from God. Readers today hear an echo in his words—the Lord does judge wickedness, yet His mercy waits always for those who turn. We are not sealed in judgment until we refuse grace itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
